opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's quite possible that they're discovering something, but I'd be careful about how much we read into it. When you train a very large circuit on an enormous amount of data, gradient descent will find whatever regularities make the loss go down, and some of those regularities will look like generalization. The question is what kind of generalization, and how robust it is.

My concern is that circuits are a fundamentally limited representation. A circuit is basically a fixed-size, feed-forward computation. It doesn't have the expressive power of, say, first-order logic or a general programming language. So when you want to express something simple, like the rules of Go, a program can capture it in a page, but a circuit needs to approximate it piece by piece, and it may need vast numbers of examples to learn what is really a very compact concept. That's a strong hint that it isn't generalizing the way a human does.

We've seen evidence of this. Take the Go programs that people assumed were superhuman. It turned out you could construct fairly simple adversarial positions, for example a large group surrounded in a cycle, that the programs badly misjudged, and an average amateur could exploit them. That suggests the system never actually learned the concept of a group being alive or dead in a general way. It learned a patchwork that works across the distribution of positions it saw, and it fails outside that.

So yes, there's something going on inside these networks, and interpretability research may show us some interesting internal structure, little algorithms forming for particular tasks. But I'm skeptical that it amounts to the kind of systematic, compositional generalization we get from representations that have logical or programmatic structure. I suspect we'll eventually need to combine learning with those richer representations, rather than hoping that scaling circuits alone will get us there.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a genuinely interesting empirical question, and I want to be careful not to dismiss it. There's clearly something going on. When you train these very large networks, they do generalize far better than the classical theory of statistical learning would have predicted. The VC dimension of these models is enormous, they can memorize random labels, and yet they generalize. So the old story about bias-variance tradeoffs is at best incomplete.

But I'd distinguish between two claims. One is that the training process finds circuits that happen to generalize, because of some combination of implicit regularization from gradient descent, the structure of the data, and the architecture. I think there's good evidence for that, and the mechanistic interpretability people have found some lovely examples: induction heads, modular arithmetic circuits that turn out to be doing Fourier transforms, and so on. The other claim is that the networks are discovering generalization as a mechanism, in the sense that they're learning something like a general-purpose method for forming abstractions and reasoning with them. I'm much more skeptical of that.

The reason is that what we see empirically is quite patchy. The same system that appears to have learned a beautifully clean algorithm for one task will fail on a trivially different version of it. In the chess and Go work, you can find systems playing at superhuman level that are defeated by absurdly simple strategies no human club player would fall for. That's not what a generalizing mechanism looks like. It looks like a very large collection of local circuits that cover the training distribution well and degrade unpredictably outside it.

And there's a deeper point. We don't actually know what these systems are doing. That's the honest answer. Interpretability has made progress on toy problems and on small pieces of large models, but we're nowhere near being able to say "here is the mechanism by which this model generalizes." So when people say the circuits are discovering generalization, I'd ask: which circuits, what mechanism, and can you show me it operating on an input it wasn't trained on? If the answer is a few case studies and a lot of extrapolation, then we're in the position of people who have built something that works and are telling stories about why.

From the point of view of safety, that's the part that worries me. If we had a theory of why these systems generalize, we could say something about when they will and won't. Right now we're relying on empirical scaling trends, which is a bit like saying the bridge has held up so far.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s quite possible. We don’t have a sufficiently good understanding of what these systems are learning internally to rule it out. A large neural network might discover a procedure that applies across a whole class of problems, rather than simply learning a collection of particular answers. And that procedure could give it a genuine ability to generalize.

But we have to distinguish that possibility from evidence that it has actually happened. If a system performs well on a test, is that because it has discovered the underlying structure of the problem, or because the training data contains enough similar examples? Those can be quite difficult to disentangle.

What I’d like to see is an account of the mechanism: what has it learned, why does that mechanism work, and under what changes in the problem should we expect it to keep working? Otherwise, we’re observing an interesting phenomenon, but we don’t yet have a satisfactory explanation of it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s certainly possible. We don’t have a very good understanding of how these systems generalize, and it would be a mistake to assume that they’re simply memorizing everything. They clearly do acquire representations that are useful across a range of tasks.

But there are two different questions here. One is whether a learning process can discover mechanisms that support generalization. The other is whether the mechanisms it has discovered will generalize in the ways we need, particularly outside the distribution on which it was trained. Evidence for the first doesn’t automatically give you the second.

So I’m very interested in understanding what’s happening inside these networks. If we can identify the mechanisms, explain why they work, and characterize where they fail, then we’ve made scientific progress. Simply observing that a larger network performs better on another benchmark leaves a great deal unanswered.
